idiom_name: Django auto pk (AutoField/BigAutoField) or SQLAlchemy Identity column
implementation_notes: The mapper supplies the identity: Django adds an auto-incrementing primary key (AutoField/BigAutoField, selectable through DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD) to every model unless one is declared, and sets instance.pk after save() - a UUID key is written as models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False), and per the docs the database will not generate it, so the default does. SQLAlchemy maps the key column (Integer, primary_key=True, optionally Identity()/serial) and fetches server-generated values immediately after INSERT via RETURNING where the backend supports it (Case 4 of its persistence docs), falling back to a follow-up SELECT otherwise (Case 5). The classic key-generator object is replaced by the column default plus the flush.
code_sketch:
class Order(models.Model):
    id = models.UUIDField(primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4, editable=False)
    name = models.CharField(max_length=64)

o = Order(name="A-1")
o.pk           # client-side default: identity already known
o.save()       # INSERT sends the explicit key

# SQLAlchemy: server-generated key, read back on flush
id_col = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True)   # + Identity()
pitfalls: Django's pk is read-only in practice and delete() resets it to None; assigning a new pk and saving creates a second row instead of updating the first.

An unsaved instance with a database-generated key has pk == None, so caches, sets or equality checks keyed on pk collapse all new objects into one identity - document the unsaved state, or generate the key client-side.
SQLAlchemy must obtain a server-generated key at INSERT time: without RETURNING support that is a second statement, and the ORM cannot manage a row whose key it does not know.
